catalog_quote: In Rural Tok Pisin, the main stress has a very strong tendency to be on the first syllable of words. However, epenthetic vowels tend to be generally unstressed and, if the first syllable of a word contains such a vowel, the main stress usually shifts to the first non-epenthetic vowel in the word. Only a few words tend to have the main stress on other syllables than the first, even if the first syllable does not contain an epenthetic vowel. The following summarises the stress patterns of Tok Pisin in general ...: (1) with words of more than one syllable, the main stress is generally on the first syllable, unless this contains an epenthetic vowel in which case the stress is placed on the first non-epenthetic vowel of the word, e.g. bikpela ... kaikai ..., but stik [sə'tik] ... skru [səkə'ru] .... ... (2) Most words of more than two syllables which end in -an, -ap, -aut, -daun and -(e)we c…
sweep_summary: Four title-hits for tokp1240 (Tok Pisin, catalog: fixed-unreviewed, initial stress per Wurm 1985 Handbook ch. 4.2.2). Three are Glottolog computerized mis-assignments confirmed from the reference records (Li 2008 on Chaucer's Middle English metre, tagged from 'translate'; Aaron & Fionda 2014 on Spanish 'semantic prosody', tagged from 'subjective'; Brauner 1982 on Bambara tone/prosody, tagged from 'funktion') -- none concerns Tok Pisin; priority none. The one real item, Faraclas 1989 'Prosody and Creolization in Tok Pisin' (JPCL 4(1):132-139, an 8-page Short Note already on the catalog list of works to obtain), is closed everywhere checked (Unpaywall closed/no repository copy, Semantic Scholar CLOSED, Crossref full-text link redirects to the Benjamins paywall, HathiTrust JPCL v.4 1989 search-only, no archive. I read the publisher's preview of p. 132: it announces a sociophonetic study of stress and intonation in 30 Boiken and Olo speakers in Wewak (East Sepik) balanced by age, sex, schooling and L1/L2 status, argued as evidence for a creolization continuum; no stress-placement statement on that page. The held APiCS survey 22 summarizes it as stress reduction in East Sepik with females tending toward English stress patterns in creolized varieties -- so at most a refinement of the sociolectal hedge, not a challenge to the initial-stress coding. Access status: not-read, priority medium (online with a university library loginvia the Harvard library catalogue; DOI 10.1075/jpcl.4.1.11nic). No new first-hand stress statement was read; the catalog's Wurm 1985 deciding source stands.

new_statements.quote: Ton och kvantitet är inte betydelseskiljande på tok pisin. Mindre omstrukturerade former av språket faller betoningen alltid på första stavelsen. I mer omstrukturerade varianter varierar betoningen (i likhet med engelska). [p. 40] ... I flera fall har dessa uttal permanentats genom att de har uppfattats som stavelsebildande varvid betoningen har flyttats, i enlighet med regeln som säger att betoningen faller på ordets första stavelse. Ett exempel är bilas, 'utsmyckning', av engelskans "flash". [p. 42]
new_statements.translation: Tone and quantity are not meaning-distinguishing in Tok Pisin. In less restructured forms of the language the stress always falls on the first syllable. In more restructured varieties the stress varies (as in English). [p. 40] ... In several cases these pronunciations have become permanent because they [epenthetic vowels] have been perceived as syllabic, whereupon the stress has shifted, in accordance with the rule which says that stress falls on the word's first syllable. An example is bilas, 'decoration', from English "flash". [p. 42]

new_statements.relation_note: The catalog holds Tok Pisin with a rule field that is not a placement statement (initial stress, apparently a mis-filled field) and no existing stress statements, so there is no placement to agree or disagree with. Kusoffsky supplies the placement: fixed initial stress in traditional Tok Pisin, with variability in anglicized varieties. Note the source is a secondary compilation (Lund C-essay) resting on Laycock 1985b / Mühlhäusler 1985.
new_statements.rule_in_words: In traditional / less anglicized ('mindre omstrukturerade') Tok Pisin, word stress is always on the first syllable, and the rule is productive: when an epenthetic vowel creates a new first syllable (English flash > bilas) the stress moves to it. In more anglicized ('mer omstrukturerade') varieties stress is variable, following the English source words. Tone and vowel length are not contrastive.
new_statements.exceptions: The whole rule is lect-conditioned: initial stress holds for less restructured forms; anglicized varieties have variable, English-like stress. The author also notes (p. 53) a phonological weakening of word-final [m] to [n] in unstressed words (em > en), and that words in the traditional lect have at most three syllables (p. 42).
new_statements.identity_note: Kusoffsky's stress statement is lect-specific: it applies to 'mindre omstrukturerade former' (less restructured / traditional Tok Pisin) and explicitly excludes the anglicized 'mer omstrukturerade varianter', where stress varies as in English. He treats Tok Pisin as a single language (following Laycock 1985b in rejecting regional dialects) and his phonology section is a Swedish digest of Laycock 1985b and Mühlhäusler 1985 (Handbook of Tok Pisin), not fieldwork. Turégano describes Tok Pisin diachronically across all stages without singling out a dialect.

(2) The classification rests on the stress chapter of the standard 725-pp reference handbook (PL C-70, 1985), the top Glottolog grammar, corroborated by three independent earlier statements from the same research tradition; all say initial stress with epenthetic vowels skipped, secondary stress on -an/-ap/-aut/-daun/-(e)we, and a listed set of English-origin exceptions -- exactly our the primary-stress rule/the secondary-stress rule. sources.quote: The results of my sociophonetic study of stress and intonation suggest that we need a new conception of creolization, pidginization, and decreolization as stages on a single continuum, rather than as totally distinct processes. One hour of spontaneous speech was collected from each of 30 members of the Boiken and the Olo ethnolinguistic groups living in Wewak town, East Sepik Province, Papua New Guinea.
